notes.body: Early on the Master says that once God's messengers have come and the evidence has been made plain, no one has an argument against God and no one has an excuse for staying astray. I took that to mean the truth is openly available to anyone who looks. But later the same teaching is described as "precious and closely guarded, noble and hidden," reached only after limits, conditions, secrecy from one's own father, and long waits not knowing where the Master even lives. I could not reconcile the two: if the matter is deliberately hidden and guarded, how has the evidence been "made plain" so completely that no one has any excuse? The chapter presses both at once and never shows me how a hidden thing still leaves the unaware without excuse.
notes.quote: no one has an excuse for remaining astray

notes.body: The Master answers the boy's challenge — why should your claim be stronger than anyone's — by dividing the world into a "we" who preserved the inheritance and a "they" who squandered it. But he never says who "we" is. The whole argument for the Master's greater right leans on this group being identifiable — "our learned instruct their ignorant," "we preserved what had been entrusted" — yet as a first-time reader I have no way to tell which people, community, or line he is placing himself inside. The claim that they need what we possess only lands if I know who "we" are, and the chapter keeps that shut. A student would ask: preserved by whom, exactly — who are the ones still holding the original inheritance?
notes.quote: they abandoned those foundations while we held fast to them
